Glikra raises 159 million euros in round led by Lobamkrar Partners, sets first overseas office opening for 6 June 2028

Travel companies that sell trips online face a familiar problem as they expand: reaching customers in a new market can be easier than arranging the local support needed when a booking changes or a journey is disrupted. Investors weighing expansion plans have to consider both sides of that business, particularly where sales are seasonal and suppliers work to different terms. Against that backdrop, Glikra, a young travel company, has raised 159 million euros in a funding round led by Lobamkrar Partners. The company says it will use the money to open its first office abroad on 6 June 2028. The announcement gives Glikra both the means to prepare for an overseas operation and a public deadline for getting it open. It does not establish how quickly the new office will generate business or what share of the funding it will need.

The lead role of Lobamkrar Partners is central to the financing announcement, although it does not by itself explain how the investment will be structured or how much influence the firm will have over the expansion. Glikra did not disclose the lead investor’s individual contribution, the valuation attached to the round or whether the financing comes with changes to the company’s board. Those distinctions matter because the size of a round is not necessarily a guide to what the lead investor paid or to the stake it acquired. For Glikra, the immediate significance is that it can begin preparing for an overseas office without treating its opening as contingent on a future fundraising announcement. “The office has a firm opening date,” a spokesperson said. The company has not named the city where the office will be located.

The opening on 6 June 2028 is the clearest milestone Glikra has set out for the expansion. It marks the start of a physical presence abroad, rather than a deadline for all of the work that might follow. A travel company can make a website available in another country without maintaining premises there, but an office brings decisions about leases, employment arrangements and which tasks should be handled locally. The announcement did not specify whether the site would serve customers directly, work mainly with suppliers or take on a mixture of those duties. Nor did it say whether the office would begin with a full complement of staff. Until Glikra publishes those details, the announced date is a firmer measure of the project’s progress than any estimate of the scale of the operation.

For the region where Glikra is based, one question is how the expansion will affect work at headquarters. A new office can shift responsibilities overseas, but it can also create work at home if local teams continue to run booking systems, handle accounts or help train staff. The company’s public profile has so far been easier to see in person than through employment forecasts: last year’s open day drew 2,168 visitors, a turnout that says more about local interest than about future staffing. Glikra has not given a hiring target linked to the round. It also has not said which responsibilities would remain with its existing teams once the overseas site opens. Without a breakdown by location and function, it is too early to translate the investment into a forecast for regional jobs.

The 159 million euros represents the amount raised, not a budget for the foreign office alone. Establishing premises and hiring staff are only part of the potential cost of entering a market. A travel business may have to adapt payment arrangements, rewrite customer information and make sure its support staff can deal with bookings under local rules. Some of that work begins before the first sale; some costs continue even during quieter periods. Glikra has not said how it plans to divide the financing between the new office and its existing operations, or how much it expects to spend before the opening. The size of the round therefore shows the scale of the financing more clearly than it shows the eventual cost of expansion. There is also no published timetable for when the overseas business might cover its own expenses.

Choosing a site will involve practical as well as commercial considerations. Staff may need to visit suppliers, and an overseas team will have to stay in contact with colleagues at home, particularly during the early stages of the move. Glikra’s headquarters is 20 kilometres from the nearest airport, a detail of its present operations that offers little guidance on where the company will choose to locate abroad. A city with good connections could make travel between offices easier, while proximity to suppliers or a suitable pool of staff might matter more for daily work. The announcement leaves open how Glikra will weigh those considerations. Disclosing a location would also make it possible to assess the local employment and consumer rules under which the office will operate, rather than assuming those conditions will match the ones familiar to the company at home.

From the investor’s perspective, leading the round puts Lobamkrar Partners at the centre of a plan whose results will take longer to assess than the opening itself. An office can start work on schedule without reaching the booking volumes needed to justify its costs. Conversely, a small operation could prove useful if it helps the company resolve disputes or retain suppliers, even before the effect shows up in sales. In travel, the amount customers pay is not the same as the amount a booking business keeps: on a hypothetical booking worth 600 euros, much of the payment might ultimately go to accommodation or transport providers. Glikra has not published figures that would allow readers to judge the expected contribution from its new market. “The opening is one step,” a person familiar with the plans said.

The funding is unlikely to change the practical questions existing customers ask first: what is included in a booking, who handles changes and how long it takes to get an answer when something goes wrong. Those questions become more important as a travel business takes on suppliers in different markets. Even a routine matter such as changing a reservation for 4 travellers may require staff to check several sets of terms before confirming the cost. Glikra’s existing office has bicycle stands outside with room for 167 bicycles, a feature of the current premises rather than an indication of the size or needs of the planned site. For customers, the more consequential detail will be whether the overseas office takes responsibility for bookings in its market or refers those cases back to the headquarters.

The choice of 6 June 2028 also gives suppliers and prospective employees a point of reference, although it does not tell them when contracts or vacancies will become available. An early summer opening may bring the office into operation during a busy booking or travel period in some markets, but demand varies by destination and by the type of trip sold. Preparation would normally have to precede the opening if staff are to answer questions and resolve problems from the start. A local team might need to learn how headquarters handles cancellations, while existing teams may have to adjust their procedures to account for different local requirements. Glikra has stated the date for opening the office, not a timetable for signing suppliers, recruiting employees or introducing any new services. Those steps will provide a fuller picture of what the launch involves.

Beyond the premises and staffing, the expansion raises a question about how much of Glikra’s existing way of doing business can carry over to a new market. Common systems can help keep booking records and customer policies consistent, but local practices can affect when travellers expect to pay and how they seek help. A deposit of 15%, for instance, would leave most of the price to be collected later, creating a different set of administrative demands from payment in full at the time of booking. That is an illustration of the choices travel businesses face, not a policy announced by Glikra. The company has not said whether its new office will have discretion over commercial terms. That decision could affect how quickly staff can respond to local suppliers and how much oversight remains with headquarters.

For local suppliers, the round could create opportunities if Glikra buys services for an expanded operation, but the announcement does not identify contracts or commit spending to the region. A business preparing to serve another market might buy more support from existing providers, select new ones near the overseas office or do both. The same uncertainty applies to the effect on day-to-day activity at headquarters: some work needed before the opening may be temporary, while functions such as booking support could require a continuing commitment. The role of Lobamkrar Partners is clearer than those purchasing and staffing decisions. It led the investment, but nothing disclosed about the round establishes where the proceeds will ultimately be spent. Local businesses assessing the possible effect will have more to go on when Glikra gives details of recruitment and procurement.

The next evidence of progress is likely to be more concrete than the financing announcement: a location, an account of what the team will do and some indication of how work will be divided between the two offices. Those details would allow residents and suppliers to assess the effect on headquarters, and give customers a clearer idea of whether they will deal with a local team when booking or seeking help. Longer-term results will be harder to judge until the office has operated through both busy and quieter periods. For now, what Glikra has disclosed is a round of 159 million euros led by Lobamkrar Partners and a commitment to open its first office abroad on 6 June 2028. The amount of funding and the opening date are settled points in the announcement; the scale and responsibilities of the new operation remain to be set out.
